slides.text:
Genetic Variation
Dr Nadine Wehida
Senior Lecturer in Genetics and Molecular Biology

Learning outcomes:
o Recap basic genetic concepts
o Mutation versus polymorphism
o Understand the various types of variations and their 
outcomes
o Identify diseases arising from various mutations

What is 
genetics?
• The scientific  study of heredity -
process in  which a parent  passes 
certain genes onto their  children.
• What does that mean?
• Children inherit their  biological 
parents’  genes that express  specific 
traits, such as  some physical  
characteristics and  genetic 
disorders.
DIPLOID CELL CHROMOSOMES

What is you Genome?
• The entire set of DNA instructions found in a cell. 
• In humans, consists of 23 pairs of chromosomes located in the 
cell’s nucleus, as well as a small chromosome in the cell’s 
mitochondria.
• Contains all the information needed for an individual to develop 
and function.
FUN FACT!
About 1-2% of our entire genome is actually coding!

Important Genetic Concepts
TERM
DEFINITION
Gene
Region of DNA that helps determine a characteristic
Allele
One of two or more alternate forms of a gene
Locus
Specific place of an allele on a chromosome 
Genotype
Set of alleles possessed by an individual organism
Heterozygote
An individual organism possessing two different alleles at 
a locus
Homozygote
An individual organism possessing two of the same alleles 
at a locus
Phenotype/ trait
The appearance or manifestation of a character

Some Important Genetic Terms
Important Genetic Concepts

Gene vs Allele
• A gene is a stretch of DNA or 
RNA that determines a specific 
trait.
• An allele brings variations to a 
single trait.

A pair of homologous chromosomes
• As a result of mutations, a gene can 
differ among individuals in terms of its 
DNA sequence. The differing sequences 
are referred to as alleles.
• Locus: A gene’s location on a 
chromosome
• If a person has the same allele on both 
members of a chromosome 
pair=homozygote.
•  If the alleles differ in DNA sequence 
=heterozygote. 
• The combination of alleles that is 
present at a given locus is termed the 
genotype.
Locus (position 
of a gene)
Allele (alternative 
form of a  gene)

Genotype vs Phenotype
• Genotype
• The genetic makeup
• Symbolized with letters
• Tt or TT, tt
• Heterozygous or 
Homozygous
• Phenotype
• Physical appearance of  
the organism
• Expression of the trait
• Shape, size, colour, and  
behavior, short, tall,  
yellow, smooth, etc.

• Many phenotypes 
are influenced by the  
environment
Phenotype = result from
the interaction of its 
genotype and with the 
environment.
The most common phenotype in a natural population is referred 
to as:
Wildtype
PHENOTYPE AND THE ENVIRONMENT

The genetic code 
The correspondence between the linear 
sequence of 4 types of nucleic acid bases and 
the 20 types of amino acids in protein
CENTRAL DOGMA OF LIFE

DECODING THE GENETIC CODE
• Read in triplicate (CODON)-discovered by Crick and Brenner.
• Non-overlapping
• Degenerate
• Nearly universal
• 20 amino acids encoded by 4 nucleotides
64 codons – only 20 
amino acids. 
Therefore, there is 
redundancy and 
codons that do not 
code for amino 
acids (stop codons)

AMINO ACIDS 
• Humans only produce 10 AAs, the 
rest is supplied by our diet
• Proteins are essential for all cellular 
processes
• AAs charge, size, shape, reactivity, 
hydrophobicity, determines protein 
folding and stability 
AA = amino acid

DEGENERACY AND THE GENETIC CODE
•
Different words can have the same 
meaning. GCA = alanine, GCC = alanine 
Third codon mutations often have no effect on 
the AA, or if they do, they change to a similar 
AA
The genetic code has likely evolved to limit the effect of mutations

Genetic Variation
• Humans display a substantial 
amount of genetic variation.
• Traits such as height, blood 
pressure, and skin color are 
reflecting of this genetic variation.
• Disease states are also included in 
the spectrum of genetic variation

MUTATIONS
•  All genetic variation originates from the 
process known as MUTATION
• Permanent change in DNA sequence can 
be either inherited from a parent or 
acquired.
• Gene mutation: may, and often, result in a 
single base error.
• Chromosome mutation:  Visible 
chromosome change.

▪Conventionally:
➢Mutation: causes genetic diseases, relatively rare (Allele 
Frequency (AF) <1%).
➢Polymorphisms: common in populations and benign
▪Nowadays:
➢Alleles that have a frequency <1% are often called polymorphisms 
as well.
➢Many common polymorphisms influence the risks for complex, 
common diseases
Mutation vs Polymorphism
The traditional distinction between mutation (rare and disease causing) and 
polymorphism (common and benign) has become increasingly blurred.

Gene mutations could be:
1) Point mutation: 
Substitution, deletion and 
insertion
3) Insertion of transposable 
elements known as ‘jumping 
genes’
2) Changes in the number of 
copies of tri-nucleotides
e.g. (AGC)3  to (AGC)5 
Will be 
thoroughly 
discussed!

Gene mutations could also be:
Spontaneous 
or induced
Somatic or 
germ cells
In coding genes 
or non-coding 
regions.

Spontaneous and induced mutations
SPONTANEOUS MUTATIONS HAVE NO KNOWN CAUSE, 
IT IS  ACCIDENTAL, IT OCCURS IN NORMAL 
BIOLOGICAL AND CHEMICAL  PROCESS; (E.G., DNA 
REPLICATION, FREE RADICALS IN  RESPIRATION).
INDUCED MUTATIONS RESULTS FROM EXTERNAL
FACTORS. COULD  BE DUE TO NATURAL FACTORS (E.G., 
UV FROM SUN, RADIATIONS FROM COSMIC AND 
MINERALS), OR ARTIFICIAL (E.G. X-RAY) .

slides.text:
Classification based on location of mutation “gametes or somatic 
cells”
Somatic Mutation
•
Affect cells in the body other than the germ 
cells.
•
Not passed onto offspring
•
Often caused by environmental factors e.g. 
radiation, chemicals or ageing
Gamete Mutation
•
Affects germ cells only; 
•
sperm or egg cells  
•
Passed onto offspring
•
Can be spontaneous or induced by 
external factors
SOMATIC OR GERM CELLS MUTATIONS
• 10 MINUTE BREAK!

TYPES OF MUTATION
Class of mutation
Type of mutation
Description
Point mutation
Substitution
One incorrect base is added during DNA 
replication
Deletion
One or more extra nucleotides excised during DNA 
replication-can lead to a frameshift
Insertion
One or more extra nucleotides added during DNA 
replication-can lead to a frameshift
Chromosomal mutation
Inversion
One region of a chromosome is flipped and re-
inserted
Deletion
A region of chromosome is lost
Duplication 
A region of chromosome is duplicated
Translocation
Region from one chromosome is aberrantly 
attached to another chromosome
Types of base-pair variation

slides.text:
It can reduce or eliminate gene function: Loss-of-function 
Rarely, it can increase a gene activity: Gain of  function
TYPES OF MUTATION

CONSEQUENCES OF MUTATION
Missense mutation:
Base-pair substitution results 
in substitution of a different 
amino acid.
-
Conservative substitution: 
Replaces one amino acid 
with chemically similar 
amino acid (Less likely to 
affect severely= Neutral 
mutation)
-
Non-conservative mutation: 
Replaces one amino acid 
with chemically different 
amino acid (Could result in 
severe change)
Silent mutation:
Base-pair 
substitution 
results in the 
same amino 
acid (different 
codon). 
Nonsense mutation: 
Base pair substitution 
results in a stop codon 
(and shorter 
polypeptide).  The 
closer to 3’UTR, might 
still produce protein 
possessing some 
activity
Consequences of base-pair substitution

Consequences of base-pair substitution
Missense
Nonsense

Base-pair substitution: Transitions Vs  
transversions

Transition and transversion mutations
Types of point mutation
1. Transition
2. transversion
TRANSITION
TRANSVERSION
• A purine base is substituted for 
a purine base
• A pyrimidine base is substituted 
for a pyrimidine base 
• E.g. T->C, G->A
• A purine base is substituted for a 
pyrimidine base
• A pyrimidine base is substituted for a 
purine base
• E.g. G->T, C->A 
Thymine + cytosine + uracil = pyrimidines
Guanine + adenine = purines

Deletion mutations in cystic fibrosis
•
Several classes of CFTR mutations
•
DF508 is the most common deletion 
causing cystic fibrosis
•
Does not cause frameshift, but

slides.topic: CHANGE OF NUMBER OF COPIES OF TRINUCLEOTIDES
slides.text:
CHANGE OF NUMBER OF COPIES OF TRINUCLEOTIDES
Huntington’s disease is an inherited 
neurodegenerative disease.
It is presented with neuropsychiatric 
symptoms, a movement disorder,
mostly choreiform, and progressive 
cognitive impairment.
It is characterised by an increased 
CAG repeat length in the huntingtin 
gene- Repeated trinucleotide CAG 
sequence.

Indel mutation
•
Frameshift mutations:
Deletions or insertions (not divisible by 3) result in  translation of incorrect amino 
acids, stops  codons (shorter polypeptides), or read-through  of stop codons 
(longer polypeptides).
This results in complete loss of structure and  function.
•
In-frame deletion or insertion:
Deletion or insertion  of a multiple of three nucleotides that does not  alter the 
reading frame.
FRAMESHIFT MUTATIONS

Types of base pair variations (Summary)
Transition mutation (AT to GC)
Transversion mutation (CG to GC)
Missense mutation (here a transition mutation from AT to GC changes from 
lysine to glutamic acid)
Nonsense mutation -change from an amino acid to a stop codon (here a 
transversion mutation from AT to TA, changing codon from lysine to UAA stop codon

Types of base pair variations (Summary)
Neutral mutation -change from an amino to another amino acid with similar 
chemical properties  (here an AT to GC transition mutation changes the codon 
from lysine to arginine)
Silent mutation (change in codon but same amino acid is coded for (here an AT 
to GC transition in the 3rd position of the codon)
Frameshift mutation -addition or deletion of one or a few base pairs lead to change 
in reading frame (here insertion of a GC base pair scrambles the message after 
glutamine)

Mutations in non-coding sequences
1. No phenotypes.
2.  Mutations in promoters or enhancers (Affect quantity but not 
quality). e.g:
A- Binding site for transcription factor: No response to 
environmental cue.
B- Binding site for suppressor: Constitutively active gene.
C- Binding site for RNA polymerase: Block gene expression.

MUTATIONS AT 
DOCKING SITES 
OF RNA
• Ribosome binding sites.
• Splice sites (Exon-Intron) junction.
• Sites that regulate translation.
• Sites that regulate localisation of 
mRNA.

Splice-site mutations
•
Splice-site mutations: occur at 
intron–exon boundaries, alter the 
splicing signal that is necessary for 
proper excision of an intron.
•
Splice-site mutations can occur at:
1. The donor site: GT sequence 
that defines the 5′ splice site
2. The acceptor site: the AG 
sequence that defines the 3′ 
splice site.
3. Near the donor and acceptor 
sites: the excision is often 
made within the next exon, at a 
splice site located in the exon 
(cryptic splice sites).

MOLECULAR CONSEQUENCES OF MUTATION
• Gain-of-function: sometimes seen 
in dominant diseases.
• Loss of function: seen in recessive 
diseases
• Haploinsufficiency: Loss of 
function seen in dominant diseases 
in which 50% of the gene product is 
insufficient for normal function.
• Dominant negative mutations: the 
abnormal protein product interferes 
with the normal protein product.

editorialNotes: Slide 35 says glutamine → valine; the sickle-cell β-globin substitution is glutamate (glutamic acid) → valine. Cards correct this and retain the original source slide.
Slide 15 gives an outdated 10/10 essential-amino-acid split. This numerical claim is not tested; standard adult human nutrition recognises nine essential amino acids.
The mutation/polymorphism frequency distinction is historical, not a rule for pathogenicity. Common variants may influence disease and rare variants may be benign.
Gene definitions refer to DNA in this human-genetics lecture; RNA genomes exist in some viruses.
Mutation effects and dominant/recessive patterns are context dependent. Frameshifts often disrupt function but are not guaranteed to cause complete loss of function.
Slide 38 is a time-dependent news clipping and is retained as a source rather than converted into clinical efficacy claims.
